sections.h: The setting and shape of the sermon
sections.b: Jesus sees the crowds, goes up a mountain and sits down, and his disciples come to him (Matthew 5:1). The sermon that follows is the first of Matthew's five long speeches. Its main body runs from "the Law or the Prophets" (Matthew 5:17) to "That is the Law and the Prophets" (Matthew 7:12): six sayings on the Law, three acts of secret devotion with the Lord's Prayer at the center, and teaching on money, worry, judging and asking. It opens with eight blessings and closes with four warnings in pairs, ending with the two builders. Luke's Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:20–49) gives a shorter form, with four blessings and four woes.

The sermon's demands, no anger, no lustful look, no oaths, no revenge, love for enemies, perfection like the Father's, have led to many readings. Medieval theology separated commands for all from "counsels" for monks and nuns. Luther separated the Christian's private life from public office, and also saw the sermon as showing everyone their need of grace. Anabaptists and Quakers read it as a rule for every believer, refusing oaths and the sword. Classic dispensationalists read it as the law of the future kingdom. Many recent interpreters stress that it begins with blessing, before any command, and that it describes the life of a community shaped by Jesus, not a way to earn salvation.

common: The sermon gathers the heart of Jesus' teaching on how his followers should live.
Jesus' authority in the sermon, "But I myself tell you," amazed his hearers (Matthew 7:28–29).
uncommon: Hans Dieter Betz argued that Matthew 5:3–7:27 is an older Jewish-Christian summary of Jesus' teaching, used by Matthew whole.
Classic dispensationalists held that the sermon applies chiefly to the future kingdom, not directly to the church.

claude.title: The Beatitudes as a portrait
claude.body: Read after the whole Gospel, each Beatitude describes Jesus himself: gentle (Matthew 11:29), mourning over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37), merciful, persecuted, and called Son of God at the cross (Matthew 27:54). The blessings may be meant as a sketch of the one who speaks them.

sections.h: Gehenna in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.b: Jesus names Gehenna three times in the sermon. Calling a brother "You idiot!" puts one in danger of "the fire of Gehenna" (Matthew 5:22), and twice he says it is better to lose an eye or a hand than to have one's whole body thrown into Gehenna (Matthew 5:29–30). The warnings are addressed to disciples, not outsiders, and use deliberate exaggeration to show how seriously God takes anger and lust. In Jesus' time Jewish writings already used Gehenna for the place where the wicked are punished after judgment (1 Enoch 27:1–3; 4 Ezra 7:36).

sections.h: Was Gehenna a burning garbage dump?
sections.b: Many sermons say the Valley of Hinnom was Jerusalem's burning rubbish heap in Jesus' day, and that this is where the image of fire came from. The earliest known source for the claim is a comment by the rabbi David Kimhi on Psalm 27:13, around AD 1200. No ancient source and no excavation confirms a dump there in the first century. The image of fire comes instead from the prophets: Jeremiah's valley of slaughter (Jeremiah 7:31–32) and the final lines of Isaiah, where the bodies of rebels lie with an undying worm and an unquenchable fire (Isaiah 66:24).

common: Gehenna names the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place of child sacrifice that became a name for final punishment.
uncommon: Some Christians, including many universalists and annihilationists, read Gehenna as destruction or as a purifying fire, not endless torment.

sections.b: Matthew sets the prayer at the center of the Sermon on the Mount, in the teaching on prayer in secret (Matthew 6:5–15). It has an address ("Our Father, who is in heaven"), three requests for God's honor (name, kingdom, will) and three for the community's needs (bread, forgiveness, rescue). Its wording echoes Jewish prayers such as the Kaddish. Jesus adds a comment on only one line: forgiveness received depends on forgiveness given (Matthew 6:14–15). The meaning of the word in "our bread for the coming day" is still debated; see the chapter page on Matthew 6.

"For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen" is not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew. An early form appears in the Didache (Didache 8:2), and most scholars think it began as a response in worship, modeled on prayers like David's (1 Chronicles 29:11), and was then copied into the text. Protestants usually say it; Catholics say it at Mass after a short prayer; the Orthodox priest sings it.

common: The prayer is used in worship by nearly every Christian tradition.
uncommon: Some scholars think "bread for the coming day" asks for a share now in the bread of the kingdom to come.

claude.title: A hinge in the chapter
claude.body: The first three requests answer the hypocrites' wish for an audience, and the last three answer the worries about food, wealth and the evil eye in the rest of Matthew 6.

sections.h: Jesus and the Law in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.b: "Do not suppose I came to do away with the Law or the Prophets" (Matthew 5:17): Jesus says not one iota will drop out of the Law and that his followers must keep it more deeply than the scribes and Pharisees. Six times he quotes a command or a common reading of it and adds his own word. Christians have read "fulfill" in many ways: Jesus obeys it, brings out its full meaning, completes what it pointed to, or replaces parts of it. Jewish scholars note that his teaching on anger, lust and oaths has close parallels among the rabbis.

common: Jesus affirms the lasting authority of the Law in Matthew 5:17–19 while claiming the authority to interpret it.
uncommon: Many critical scholars think Matthew's church still kept the whole Law, including food and Sabbath laws.

sections.h: Divorce in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.b: Jesus quotes the rule that a man who divorces his wife must give her a certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1) and says that anyone who divorces his wife "for any cause except sexual sin" makes her an adulteress, and that marrying a divorced woman is adultery (Matthew 5:31–32). The debate between the schools of Hillel and Shammai over the grounds of divorce is the background. The exception, found only in Matthew, has divided churches: most Protestants allow divorce and remarriage for adultery; the Orthodox allow divorce for adultery and remarriage by pastoral "economy"; the oldest Western reading, from Jerome and Augustine, and Catholic teaching since Trent allow separation but not remarriage.

The Law forbade swearing falsely by God's name (Leviticus 19:12) and required vows to be kept. Jesus forbids oaths entirely: not by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or one's own head, because all belong to God. A plain yes or no is to be enough (Matthew 5:33–37; compare James 5:12). Anabaptists and Quakers refuse all oaths on this basis; most churches allow oaths required by courts and governments.

Jesus quotes "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" and tells his disciples not to set themselves against the evil person: turn the other cheek, give your outer robe too, go the second mile, give to those who ask (Matthew 5:38–42). The law set limits for judges; Jesus speaks to the person wronged. Readings range from a ban on personal revenge only, to complete nonviolence, to Walter Wink's view that the examples teach nonviolent resistance.

"Love your neighbor" (Leviticus 19:18) was commonly read as love for fellow Israelites. Jesus quotes it with the addition "and hate your enemy," which is not in the Law but echoes attitudes of the time (the Qumran Community Rule tells members to hate "the sons of darkness"). He commands love and prayer for enemies, after the example of the Father, who sends sun and rain on all (Matthew 5:43–48). The Golden Rule then sums up the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 7:12).

Jesus warns against praying to be seen and against piling up words as if God needed to be worn down. Disciples are to pray to their Father in private, trusting that he knows their needs before they ask (Matthew 6:5–8). Later in the sermon he urges them to keep asking, looking and knocking, because the Father gives good things (Matthew 7:7–11).

Jesus assumes his disciples will give to the poor, but they must not do it for show: "keep your left hand from knowing what your right hand does" (Matthew 6:3). The Father who sees in secret will repay. Jewish teaching also praised secret giving; the Temple had a "chamber of secrets" where the devout left gifts and the poor drew support without shame (Mishnah Shekalim 5:6).

Jesus expects his disciples to fast but tells them to oil their hair and wash their faces so that only the Father sees (Matthew 6:16–18). The devout fasted on Mondays and Thursdays; the Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays instead (Didache 8:1). The passage is read on Ash Wednesday in many Western churches.

Jesus warns against piling up treasure on earth, where moths, rust and thieves destroy it, and says the heart follows the treasure. "You cannot be a slave both to God and to wealth" (Matthew 6:24): the Aramaic word behind "wealth," mammon, meant property or money, here pictured as a rival master. He then tells the disciples to stop worrying about food and clothes and to seek God's kingdom first (Matthew 6:25–34).

Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with pairs: a narrow gate and a wide one, a cramped road to life and a roomy road to ruin, good and rotten trees, a house on rock and a house on sand (Matthew 7:13–27). The pattern follows Moses' choice of life and death (Deuteronomy 30:15–20) and Psalm 1. The Didache, an early Christian manual, opens with "There are two ways, one of life and one of death" (Didache 1:1).

Jesus warns against false prophets who look like sheep but are wolves, and gives a test: their fruit (Matthew 7:15–20). Some will call him "Lord, Lord," prophesy and work miracles in his name, but he will say, "I never knew you," because they did not do his Father's will (Matthew 7:21–23). Most scholars think Matthew had in mind Christian prophets in his own churches.

sections.h: The kingdom in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.b: The sermon begins and ends its blessings with the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:3, 10), warns that only a greater righteousness enters it (Matthew 5:20), teaches the disciples to pray "May your kingdom come" (Matthew 6:10), tells them to seek it before anything else (Matthew 6:33), and warns that not all who say "Lord, Lord" will enter (Matthew 7:21). Matthew usually says "kingdom of heaven," a reverent Jewish way of saying "kingdom of God."

The six sayings on the Law end with the call to be perfect as the heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48), a reworking of "Be holy, because I am holy" (Leviticus 19:2). The Greek word means whole or complete; Luke's parallel has "merciful" (Luke 6:36). Churches differ on whether Christian perfection can be reached in this life.

Matthew's first Beatitude blesses "the poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3); Luke's simply "you poor" (Luke 6:20). Both draw on Isaiah 61:1, good news for the poor. The Dead Sea Scrolls use "poor in spirit" for the humble faithful (War Scroll 14:7). Readers have long debated whether Matthew spiritualized Luke or both express the biblical "poor," the needy who depend on God.

The fourth Beatitude blesses those who "are hungry and thirsty for righteousness" (Matthew 5:6). The Greek word can mean both right living and justice: the hungry may be those who long to do God's will, or those who long for God to set the world right, as the poor and persecuted around them did. The sermon later warns not to perform "righteousness" for show (Matthew 6:1), and tells the disciples to seek God's righteousness before anything else (Matthew 6:33).

sections.h: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs"
sections.b: The early Christian manual called the Didache applies Jesus' saying "Do not give what is holy to the dogs" (Matthew 7:6) to the Eucharist: only the baptized may eat (Didache 9:5). The verse has been cited ever since in debates over closed and open communion.

In the Lord's Prayer sins are debts (Matthew 6:12), as in Aramaic, where the word hova means both. Luke's version has "sins" in the first half and "everyone who owes us" in the second (Luke 11:4). For poor Galileans, many in real debt, the image was vivid; Jesus' parable of the unforgiving slave (Matthew 18:23–35) develops it.

sections.h: "Do not set yourself against the evil person"
sections.b: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus tells his disciples not to resist the evil person, to turn the other cheek and to love and pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:38–48). These words are the main source of Christian pacifism. Augustine and Luther read them as rules for personal life, not for rulers, soldiers and judges, who may use force to protect others. The Anabaptists (Schleitheim Confession, 1527), the Quakers and the other peace churches read them as binding on every believer, so that Christians may not take up the sword. Catholic teaching sets limits on war through the conditions of a just war (Catechism 2309) and asks states to provide for conscientious objectors.

common: Nearly all churches agree that Jesus forbids personal revenge.
uncommon: Walter Wink read the examples in Matthew 5:39–41 as strategies of nonviolent resistance rather than submission.
